title: Security assessment: protocol-ctf lab servers
boundary: The nine lab servers under protocol-ctf/challenges/ (WebSocket, gRPC and AI-agent tracks), each bound to 127.0.0.1. Remediation was assessed against the reference fixes in protocol-ctf/solutions/.

tester.name: security-research maintainers
tester.independence: Not independent: the testers also wrote the lab servers. This is a dogfood engagement to exercise the report tooling. A client engagement would use a tester independent of the code's authors.

methodology: Static analysis with our ESLint security plugins at their strict configs. Then manual exploitation of each server with the reference exploit, a negative control to confirm the exploit is what gets the flag, and a retest of the reference fix: the functional check must pass and the exploit must be blocked.
limitations: The labs are intentionally vulnerable. Findings are real for this code but were placed on purpose. AI-track servers use a deterministic toy model, not a production LLM.
outOfScope: The CTF CLI (ctf.mjs), shared libraries under lib/, dependencies, and deployment. The labs run only on loopback.
summary: The nine lab servers contain nine exploitable vulnerabilities, all confirmed by exploitation. Four are critical: command injection in the MCP tool server, code injection in the gRPC order filter, prototype pollution granting admin, and identity spoofing through gRPC metadata. A reference fix for each was verified to block the exploit while keeping the feature working. A tenth weakness, a non-constant-time password comparison in the chat server, is low severity and remains open in both the vulnerable and the fixed code. The labs are intentionally vulnerable: these results describe the code as written, not a production deployment.

confidentiality: Internal: prepared for the security-research project. Not for distribution outside it.
rulesOfEngagement: Testing ran only against the lab servers on 127.0.0.1, on a workstation controlled by the testers. No third-party system, account or network was touched. Exploits were run only against the intentionally vulnerable lab code.
strategicRecommendations: Never pass client-influenced strings to a shell, an evaluator or a dynamic-code constructor. F-01 and F-06 share this root cause.
Derive identity only from verified credentials. Headers, metadata and Origin are client-controlled (F-04, F-08).
Check authorization on every message and object, not only at connection time (F-07).
Give AI agents only the tools their task needs, and keep secrets out of prompts (F-02, F-03).
positiveObservations: Every server binds to 127.0.0.1 only, so none of the findings is reachable from the network in the lab as shipped.
Every vulnerability has an exploit, a negative control and a reference fix, checked by one command. That gives this assessment a reproducible evidence chain.
The flag secret is created with owner-only permissions (0600).

timeline.event: Static analysis of the nine servers with the ESLint security plugins (strict)
Manual exploitation of each server, with a negative control per exploit
Reference fixes verified: functional check passes and exploit blocked

revisions.change: Adds difficulty, exploit scenarios, coverage and document control. Reference fixes are now labeled as such, not as client retests. SOC 2 mapping narrowed.

coverage.test: OS command injection through MCP tool arguments (ai-1)
Indirect prompt injection against the digest agent and its tool permissions (ai-2)
System prompt secret extraction past input and output filters (ai-3)
Service enumeration through gRPC reflection and unauthenticated internal methods (grpc-2)
Code injection through the order filter expression (grpc-3)
WebSocket Origin validation and its use as authentication (ws-2)
Password comparison and storage in the chat login (ws-1)
Every server listens on loopback only
Flag secret stored with owner-only file permissions
